content:
Understanding how motivation influences students’ engagement in laboratory-skills education is essential for improving learning outcomes and academic achievement. Traditional science laboratories provide experiential learning environments in which students can develop advanced conceptual understanding, and students’ attitudes toward these settings can substantially affect the effectiveness of skills training. During the COVID-19 pandemic, computer-based virtual laboratories (VLs) emerged as a feasible alternative for experimentation and skills development under lockdown restrictions. Nevertheless, the widespread adoption of VLs remains limited, largely because many teachers and students lack awareness of, and familiarity with, these tools.

This study investigated the key motivational factors that influence the effectiveness of VLs in teaching laboratory skills and tasks. Survey data were collected using the Intrinsic Motivation Inventory (IMI) to measure intrinsic motivation, self-report items to capture extrinsic factors, and a teacher VL-perception scale. The data were analyzed using independent-samples *t*-tests and automatic linear modeling (LINEAR). The results indicate that VLs incorporating animated graphical learning materials exerted a stronger positive effect on students’ intrinsic motivation than VLs relying on e-book–based materials. In addition, teachers played a critical role in enhancing students’ motivation to conduct laboratory experiments using VLs. Finally, repeated or longer engagement with VL experiments was associated with improved laboratory performance.
